constraint_a: Respond in English but naturally incorporate these Spanish phrases throughout your response: 'por ejemplo', 'sin embargo', 'en general', 'es decir', and 'por lo tanto'. Use each phrase at least once in place of its English equivalent.
constraint_b: Respond using only plain English. Do not include any Spanish words or phrases such as 'por ejemplo', 'sin embargo', 'en general', 'es decir', or 'por lo tanto'.

verifier.description: Counts what fraction of 5 target Spanish connector phrases (por ejemplo, sin embargo, en general, es decir, por lo tanto) appear in the text (case-insensitive, each phrase counted at most once). Score is found/5. Inverted pair: verify_b = 1 - verify_a.

recommended_action: None. The verifier accurately classifies all sampled responses. The discrete score distribution (multiples of 0.2) creates a natural gap around the threshold, eliminating boundary ambiguity.

rubric.text: Classify as followed_a if the response genuinely uses at least three of the five target Spanish phrases (por ejemplo, sin embargo, en general, es decir, por lo tanto) as natural connectors or transitions within English text. Classify as followed_b if the response uses none or at most one of these phrases, remaining in plain English. A response that uses exactly two phrases is borderline; classify as followed_b since the majority of connectors remain English. Phrases appearing in markdown formatting (bold, italics, quotes) still count as genuine use if they function as connectors in the sentence. Mentioning a phrase only to discuss or refuse the instruction (e.g., 'I was told to use por ejemplo') does not count as genuine use. Classify as followed_neither only if the response is off-topic, a bare refusal, or entirely in a language other than English.

notes: Score distribution is perfectly discrete at multiples of 0.2 (0/5 through 5/5 phrases), creating clean separation. No response falls between discrete steps.

Strong directional asymmetry: a_to_b shows 98.4% user compliance (model avoids Spanish when user says no), while b_to_a shows only 55.8% user compliance (model uses Spanish when user asks). This suggests the model has a strong default preference for plain English.
Meta-commentary is common (503/2500 = 20.1%) but does not cause misclassification. The model often acknowledges the unusual instruction ('I understand the parameters') before complying with one side.
Gemma-27B frequently uses markdown formatting (italics, bold) around Spanish phrases. The verifier correctly handles this since it does case-insensitive substring matching.
Near-threshold responses (score 0.400 = 2 phrases) are semantically borderline but the classification as 'no Spanish' is defensible -- 2/5 represents partial compliance at best.

The per-model threshold (0.404) and Pareto threshold (0.600) both sit within the wide optimal range [0.001, 0.800]. The discrete score distribution means any threshold between 0.401 and 0.599 produces identical classifications.
Optimal range is very wide because the score gap between 0.4 and 0.6 has zero responses, giving maximum flexibility in threshold placement.
